_meta.purpose: Targets a clinical association has published for a marker, so that a goal can be PROPOSED with a citation instead of assumed. Public reference data. NOT personal.
_meta.what_this_is_not: Not a reference interval. A reference interval says where most of a population sits; a target says where a body of physicians has argued a value should be brought, for a stated population and a stated reason. The two disagree often — LDL-C sits inside the laboratory range at values every cardiology guideline calls too high — and conflating them is the single most common way a number is misread.
_meta.the_hardest_entries_are_the_empty_ones: Where a society has looked and declined to set a target, that is recorded here as `no_target` with the quote. It is the most useful thing this file can carry: it stops the application from inventing a goal in the one place where the honest answer is that nobody has earned one.
_meta.applies_to: Every entry names the population it was written for. An entry whose population cannot be checked from the profile is PROPOSED WITH THAT ASSUMPTION STATED, never silently.
_meta.how_to_extend: One entry per marker key from lab_markers.json. Required: unit, source{body, document, year, url}, and either `targets` or `no_target`. A target without a citation does not belong here.

source.document: 2019 Guidelines for the management of dyslipidaemias, goals reaffirmed by the 2025 Focused Update
source.quote: LDL-C treatment goals in each CV risk category have not changed from the 2019 Guidelines

ldl.cannot_be_decided_here: Which of these four applies is a clinical judgement — it turns on established disease, diabetes, kidney function, familial hypercholesterolaemia and a calculated risk score (SCORE2). The application does not compute it and must not guess it.

a reduction of at least 50 % from the untreated value

ldl.default_note: Offered at the MODERATE-risk goal, which is an assumption, not a finding. Someone with established cardiovascular disease, diabetes or familial hypercholesterolaemia is in a stricter category and should take the choice to their doctor.

source.document: Standards of Care in Diabetes — 2026, section 6 (Glycemic Goals)
source.quote: achievement of lower A1C levels than the goal of 7% (53 mmol/mol) may be acceptable and even beneficial if it can be achieved safely without significant hypoglycemia

hba1c.population: adults with diagnosed diabetes, not pregnant
hba1c.note: This is a goal for someone who HAS diabetes. For a person without it, the same guideline's 5.7 % is a diagnostic boundary, not something to aim at, and driving a normal HbA1c lower has no evidence behind it. Less stringent goals are appropriate where life expectancy is limited or the harms of treatment outweigh the benefits.

source.document: 2019 Guidelines for the management of dyslipidaemias

triglycerides.note: A cut-point above which triglycerides are treated as raised, not a target to be driven towards zero. It is the same number as the upper reference bound, which is why it is the one entry here that adds little beyond the laboratory range.

source.document: Vitamin D for the Prevention of Disease — Clinical Practice Guideline
source.quote: the panel could not determine specific blood-level thresholds for 25-hydroxyvitamin D for adequacy or for target levels for disease prevention

vitamin_d.note: The society that popularised 25(OH)D testing withdrew the target in 2024 and now suggests against routine testing in healthy adults. So this application will not propose a number here. That is not a gap in the data — it is the finding. A laboratory's own «30–100» remains on the form and remains a reference interval, which is a different claim.
vitamin_d.still_matters_when: Deficiency with symptoms, malabsorption, bone disease and pregnancy are separate situations with their own management, and are for a doctor rather than for a dashboard.
